Seattle, Washington · ride

Bike routes in Seattle

The rides locals in Seattle actually do, each with a route you can load.

Best months: July, the driest month: an average high near 77°F and less than an inch of rain (WeatherSpark).

More on when to ride

The Seattle to Portland Bicycle Classic leaves the University of Washington the second weekend of July. Cascade Bicycle Club’s free group rides go out all year, and the club requires full fenders on its rides when the roads are wet. Its season opens on Bainbridge Island with Chilly Hilly in February; the event page says to wear layers and be ready for rain.

Bike routes in Seattle, listed

What do you need?

  1. Lake Washington loop

    • Road
    • 50 mi
    • 1,900 ft up
    • Hard
    • Start: South Bellevue Park and Ride, off Bellevue Way, Bellevue
    • Water: Stops the club’s page names: Log Boom Park in Kenmore, Seward Park in Seattle and Gene Coulon Park in Renton. It doesn’t say which have water.
    • Watch: From the club’s page: the downtown Bellevue stretch may be safer on the sidewalk, depending on the time of day.
    Route on RideWithGPSRoute pageTo the start
    More about Lake Washington loop

    The lap of the lake: counter-clockwise from Bellevue, north through Kirkland and Kenmore, down the Seattle shore past Seward Park, and back through Renton. 50 miles and about 1,900 feet, per Cascade Bicycle Club’s RideWithGPS ambassador route. No steep climbs; most of the climbing is in the first half, on the Eastside. It’s a loop, so from Seattle join it on the lakeshore, at Seward Park for one. Some of it is hard to follow, the club says, so study the map first. Cascade’s MUMPS ride (Mondays, 10:00 am) leaves Log Boom Park, one of the stops the club names, for loops of the lake’s north end and Mercer Island.

    Surface: A mix of trail and road, per Cascade’s route page.

    Watch: Seattle’s roads are in poor shape. Cross the railroad tracks in Renton at 90 degrees. Check the University of Washington section before you go; construction there has meant detours. Don’t leave valuables in your car at the South Bellevue lot.

  2. The Burke-Gilman Trail

    Seattle’s rail-trail, one of the first in the country, per Cascade.

    • Path
    • 19 mi
    • Easy
    • Start: Gas Works Park, one of the access points King County names
    • Watch: It’s shared with everyone on foot: all non-motorized uses are allowed, King County says. In Ballard the trail leaves the path for a stretch on the road.

    Ride it with the group: LUMPS (Leisurely Urbane Matthews-beach Pedalers) (Wednesdays, 11:30 am) →

    Route pageTo the start
    More about The Burke-Gilman Trail

    It runs from Golden Gardens and Shilshole Bay past the Ballard Locks, Fremont, Gas Works Park, the University of Washington and Magnuson Park to Bothell, where it meets the Sammamish River Trail. About 19 miles, per Cascade; King County says more than 20. This is the ride for the evening you land: no cars, turn around whenever you want. If you’re in town for the STP, it runs past the start on the UW campus. Cascade’s LUMPS ride (Wednesdays, 11:30 am) leaves Matthews Beach Park, on the trail, for a pie stop in Bothell. PIM Bicycles & Coffeehouse in Fremont and Fremont Brewing’s beer garden sit a block off it (see Coffee and Off the bike); Matthews Beach is the swim.

    Surface: Paved, with a soft-surface shoulder, except an on-road stretch in Ballard.

  3. North Lake Washington trail loop (Burke-Gilman, Sammamish River, 520)

    • Path
    • 35 mi
    • 1,100 ft up
    • Moderate
    • Start: Log Boom Park, Kenmore, 17415 61st Ave NE, Kenmore, WA 98028
    • Watch: About 3 miles are on roads with traffic, per the club.
    Route pageTo the start
    More about North Lake Washington trail loop (Burke-Gilman, Sammamish River, 520)

    The north end of the lake almost all on trail: the Burke-Gilman to Bothell, the Sammamish River Trail to Redmond, and the SR 520 Trail back over the 520 bridge to Montlake. 35 miles and about 1,100 feet, per Cascade’s ride page; the club’s ride started at Log Boom Park in Kenmore, with restrooms at the start and along the way. It’s a loop, so start where you’re staying. Seattle Bike Blog rode a 32-mile version from UW Station, on the light rail, that uses the Eastrail and the Cross Kirkland Corridor on the east side; that version has about 7.5 miles of hard-packed gravel. Log Boom Park is where Cascade’s MUMPS ride (Mondays, 10:00 am) meets.

    Surface: Mostly paved trail, with about 3 miles on roads with traffic, per the club.

    Watch: On the Seattle Bike Blog’s Eastrail version, the blog named the Eastrail crossing at 132nd Ave NE and the stretch of 108th Ave NE near South Kirkland Park and Ride as the weak spots (July 2023).

  4. Mercer Island loop

    Across the I-90 bridge to Mercer Island, a clockwise lap of the island, and back on the Mountains to Sound Greenway trail.

    • Road
    • 17 mi
    • 1,000 ft up
    • Moderate
    • Start: South Bellevue Park and Ride, off Bellevue Way, Bellevue
    • Water: On the route, per the club’s points of interest: a QFC grocery and a Starbucks on the island, the Roanoke Inn, and bathrooms at Lid Park.
    • Watch: Stop signs on the island are patrolled.
    Route on RideWithGPSRoute pageTo the start
    More about Mercer Island loop

    17 miles and about 1,000 feet, per Cascade’s RideWithGPS ambassador route (the route page itself says 16.5 miles). Rolling, with one real climb and descent. The club calls the island roads low-traffic, with few turns and a good shoulder. Lid Park, on the I-90 lid, has bathrooms and the view. The Roanoke Inn, the tavern the club’s page tells riders to stop at, is a few blocks off the trail at the island’s north end (see Restaurants).

    Surface: Paved road and trail.

    Watch: Come to a full stop, the club says. Where the trail meets a road, check for cars. Don’t leave valuables in your car at the South Bellevue lot; the club says it has no cameras.

  5. Zoo Hill (Cougar Mountain)

    The Eastside’s climb: Cascade built a ride around Cougar Mountain’s Zoo Hill, a 9-mile loop from Lewis Creek Park with about 1,450 feet of climbing.

    • Climb
    • 9 mi
    • 1,450 ft up
    • Hard
    • Start: Lewis Creek Park, upper parking lot, Bellevue, 5808 Lakemont Blvd SE, Bellevue, WA 98006
    • Water: Lewis Creek Park at the start (water and bathrooms, per the club).
    • Watch: The club’s page says nothing about traffic on the road or the descent; the grade is the hazard. Expect 8 to 13 percent most of the way and pitches to 18.
    Route pageTo the start
    More about Zoo Hill (Cougar Mountain)

    The grade runs from 3 to 18 percent, mostly 8 to 13, and there’s no flat: in the club’s words, “you’re either going up, or down.” If you have more in you, the club adds Newport to 164th or the Lakemont hill after. The ride page is from 2018; the hill hasn’t moved. To climb with a group, Cascade’s Eastside Hills ride (Saturdays, 10:00 am) picks a new hilly route east of the lake each week.

    Surface: Paved road.

  6. Snoqualmie Valley Trail gravel loop from Carnation

    • Gravel
    • 38 mi
    • 1,200 ft up
    • Moderate
    • Start: Tolt MacDonald Park, Carnation, 31020 NE 40th St, Carnation, WA 98014
    • Water: Restrooms and water at the Snoqualmie Falls viewpoint, about mile 23; restrooms at the start (club page).
    • Watch: The club’s page names no hazards.
    Route pageTo the start
    More about Snoqualmie Valley Trail gravel loop from Carnation

    Cascade’s gravel ride in the Snoqualmie Valley: south on the Snoqualmie Valley Trail to North Bend, paved roads to the Snoqualmie Falls viewpoint, back on the trail to Fall City, then paved roads home to Carnation. 38 miles and about 1,200 feet, about half of it gravel, per the club (Sept 2023). Cascade calls the trail an easy first gravel ride, with farmland and river views. On the club’s rides, full fenders are required when the roads are wet. Cascade’s TREATS ride (Tuesdays, 10:00 am) often heads out to the valley with a lunch stop.

    Surface: About 19 miles of gravel trail, the rest paved road. The club asks for tires of at least 28mm.

    Watch: Half the loop is gravel trail, so 28mm tires at least, and fenders when it’s wet, per the club. Carnation is out in the Snoqualmie Valley; this one wants a car or a long ride out.

  7. Bainbridge Island by ferry (the Chilly Hilly course)

    Roll onto the Bainbridge ferry at Colman Dock on the downtown waterfront and ride the Chilly Hilly course.

    • Road
    • 33 mi
    • 2,150 ft up
    • Moderate
    • Start: Colman Dock, the Seattle ferry terminal, 801 Alaskan Way, Seattle, WA 98104
    • Water: Battle Point Park, about mile 14 (restrooms and water, per Cascade’s midsummer ride page). Restrooms on the ferry.
    • Watch: All public roads, open to traffic. On event day, traffic officers work the highway crossings; on your own, nobody does. In February, Cascade’s page says to wear layers and be ready for rain.
    Route on RideWithGPSRoute pageTo the start
    More about Bainbridge Island by ferry (the Chilly Hilly course)

    It’s a 33-mile loop of the island: the shore road with Seattle behind you, back roads through the trees, and the hills it’s named for. About 2,150 feet, per Cascade’s 2026 event page; a RideWithGPS copy of the course says 32.8 miles and 2,290 feet. It’s the course of Cascade’s February season opener, and the club has led it as a midsummer ride too. Return ferries run on the regular Washington State Ferries schedule. Pegasus Coffee House in Winslow is the coffee off the boat (see Coffee); Bainbridge Bike Co is steps from the terminal and Classic Cycle a mile up the hill (see Bike shops). The ferry fare and how bikes board are on the Bring-your-bike page.

    Surface: Paved public roads.

  8. West Seattle loop (Lincoln Park and Alki)

    Cascade’s 12-mile clockwise loop of West Seattle from Seacrest Pier, past Lincoln Park and along Alki.

    • Road
    • 12 mi
    • 450 ft up
    • Easy
    • Start: Seacrest Pier, West Seattle, 1660 Harbor Ave SW, Seattle, WA 98126
    • Watch: The club’s page names no hazards. The first half is the climbing. If you cross on the water taxi, the boat has a limited number of bike racks, per Cascade.
    Route pageTo the start
    More about West Seattle loop (Lincoln Park and Alki)

    The first half climbs; the second half is mostly flat by the water. About 450 feet, per the club. Restrooms at Seacrest Park, start and finish. Cascade also leads a ride that crosses Elliott Bay to West Seattle on the West Seattle Water Taxi from Pioneer Square; the boat has a limited number of bike racks. Marination Ma Kai, at the pier, is lunch after (see Restaurants). The Beer Junction Bike Club’s ride (Last Saturday of the month, 2:00 pm) is the slow, short West Seattle loop from a bar on California Ave.

    Surface: Road and trail, with half a mile of crushed-rock trail that road bikes handle fine, per the club.
